tier1.customer: Breastfeeding or formula-feeding mother, 0-12 weeks postpartum, doing 100% of night care while her partner sleeps through or is minimally involved
tier1.scene: 'Can you help more?' produced a one-off gesture, not a system. He believes helping means one nappy change.
tier1.pain: Asking directly for help can feel like an accusation. The partner's one-off gesture resets the expectation: he helped once, so the default remains she owns all of it.
tier1.failed_attempt: Asking directly for help can feel like an accusation — so she stops asking, and the default quietly becomes she owns all of it.

emotional_stake.text: Rage at his calm breathing while she feeds; grief for the relationship; and fear that this is now permanent. She stops asking because naming it makes her the difficult one.

insight.text: A request creates a favour. A schedule creates a default. Giving your partner a named shift is a status upgrade, not charity.
insight.label: Strategic Synthesis

mechanism.text: Reframes the partner from 'helper' to 'co-manager' — a status upgrade instead of a request for charity. A written roster removes the emotional labour of asking: the schedule asks, not her.

tier2.desired_change: Nights with zero protected block become a protected block of 3+ hours on most nights. 'Whose turn' arguments drop from several times a week to once a week or less. The partner initiates his shift without being reminded.
tier2.angle: He believes helping means one nappy change. Asking directly for help can feel like an accusation, so you stop asking — and the default quietly becomes you own all of it. A written roster reframes him from helper to co-manager: a named shift, not charity. The schedule asks, not you.

tier3.counter_evidence_acknowledged: This is not baby sleep training, and it is not a substitute for medical or mental-health care. When exhaustion is more than tiredness, stop and route out.
